steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a theory paper on rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics for sampling proper colorings on line graphs with (1+o(1))\Delta colors, using the matrix trickle-down theorem. Cover the background conjecture and prior results, why line graphs are special, our construction and main theorems, and the paper's organization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Proper colorings, Glauber dynamics and the \Delta+2 conjecture
2. Special graph families: large girth
3. Edge colorings and line graphs
4. Matrix trickle-down theorem
5. Our construction and its advantages
6. Main results (bounded and unbounded degree), edge-coloring view
7. Organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Colorings and the conjecture
- proper (vertex) q -coloring of G=(V,E): adjacent vertices get distinct colors; \Delta = max degree
- conjecture: single-site Glauber dynamics mixes rapidly when q at least \Delta+2
- Jerrum; Salas and Sokal: rapid mixing for q\geq 2\Delta
- current best: q\geq\left(\frac{11}{6}-\epsilon_{0}\right)\Delta, \epsilon_{0}\approx 10^{-5}; still far

2. Large girth
- special graph families, most successful = large girth
- Chen, Liu, Mani and Moitra: for any \Delta\geq 3 exists \mathrm{g}>0, max degree at most \Delta, girth at least \mathrm{g} -> rapid mixing for q\geq\Delta+3
- almost solves conjecture for large girth

3. Edge colorings / line graphs
- edge coloring: adjacent edges distinct colors
- = vertex coloring of line graph (vertices = edges of G, adjacent iff incident)
- large girth "locally sparse" vs line graphs "locally dense": cliques glued, each vertex in exactly two cliques
- coupling can't exploit structure -> condition same as general graphs for a long time

4. Matrix trickle-down
- Abdolazimi, Liu and Oveis Gharan: matrix trickle-down theorem, uses structural info
- line graph colorings mix rapidly for q>\frac{10}{6}\Delta
- with "local-to-global" scheme for high-dimensional expanders -> optimal mixing time for certain chains
- generalizes trickle-down theorem (spectral gaps of local walks on links of simplicial complexes)
- looks at local walks themselves, connections between transition matrices

5. Our construction
- need matrix upper bounds for local walks, bounded spectrum, inductive inequality constraints
- main challenge: control eigenvalue magnitudes
- we: systematic study of constraints, almost optimal construction for line graph colorings
- advantages vs earlier construction: explicit; spectrum related to adjacency matrix of line graph (locally a clique); existence reduced to feasibility of inequality system, fully characterized

6. Results
- O_{\Delta}(n\log n) mixing for bounded degree, o(\Delta) extra colors
- thm: q\geq\Delta+20028\cdot\Delta/\log\Delta -> modified log-Sobolev constant \Omega_{\Delta}(1/n)
- O(n^{19/9}\log q) for degree unbounded; spectral gap larger than n^{-10/9}
- holds for list coloring; Theorem 24
- edge colorings: q\geq(2+o(1))d; line graph degree up to 2d-2
- near ergodicity threshold: reducible when q<2d
- Vizing: edge colorable for q\geq d+1; rapid mixing under same condition known for trees

7. Organization
- Section 2 notation/preliminaries; Section 2.5 matrix trickle-down
- Section 3 construction + main results
- Section 4 analysis of inequalities, maybe of independent interest

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A proper (vertex) q -coloring of a graph G=(V,E) assigns each vertex one of q colors so that adjacent vertices always get distinct colors. Let \Delta be the maximum degree of G. It is widely conjectured that the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling proper colorings on G uniformly mixes rapidly whenever the number of colors q is at least \Delta+2. The seminal work of Jerrum and Salas and Sokal showed that Glauber dynamics is rapidly mixing when q\geq 2\Delta, and after that a number of works tried to resolve the conjecture. The current best bound needs q\geq\left(\frac{11}{6}-\epsilon_{0}\right)\Delta for some \epsilon_{0}\approx 10^{-5}, and this is still far from what we want.

Another way to approach the conjecture is to look at special graph families, and the most successful cases are graphs with large girths. In a very recent work of Chen, Liu, Mani and Moitra, it was proven that for any \Delta\geq 3 there is a \mathrm{g}>0 such that for any graph G with maximum degree at most \Delta and girth at least \mathrm{g}, the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling proper q -colorings on G mixes rapidly whenever q\geq\Delta+3. This result almost solves the conjecture for large girth graphs.

A closely related problem is sampling proper edge colorings. Here the colors are assigned to the edges instead of the vertices, so that adjacent edges have distinct colors. A proper edge coloring of G corresponds naturally to a vertex coloring of the line graph of G, where the vertices are the edges of G and two vertices are adjacent in the line graph if and only if the corresponding edges are incident in G. So sampling proper colorings on line graphs is of particular interest. Graphs with a large girth are "locally sparse", but line graphs are "locally dense". A line graph is formed by gluing together several cliques, and each vertex belongs to exactly two cliques. Previous methods like coupling can hardly use this special structure, and so for a long time the rapid mixing condition for line graphs stayed the same as for general graphs.

In a recent breakthrough, Abdolazimi, Liu and Oveis Gharan developed a new technique for proving rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics, the matrix trickle-down theorem, which can make good use of the structural information of the underlying graphs. With it, it was shown in that work that the Glauber dynamics for sampling colorings on line graphs mixes rapidly when q>\frac{10}{6}\Delta. Together with the recent revolutionary development of the "local-to-global" scheme for high-dimensional expanders, the technique gives optimal mixing time for certain Markov chains. The matrix trickle-down theorem generalizes an earlier trickle-down theorem, which connected the spectral gaps of the local walks on links of the underlying simplicial complexes. The matrix version does not only look at the spectral gap but also at the local walks themselves, and it establishes more general connections between (the transition matrix of) local walks on links.

5. Our construction
- need matrix upper bounds for local walks, bounded spectrum, inductive inequality constraints
- main challenge: control eigenvalue magnitudes
- we: systematic study of constraints, almost optimal construction for line graph colorings
- advantages vs earlier construction: explicit; spectrum related to adjacency matrix of line graph (locally a clique); existence reduced to feasibility of inequality system, fully characterized

6. Results
- O_{\Delta}(n\log n) mixing for bounded degree, o(\Delta) extra colors
- thm: q\geq\Delta+20028\cdot\Delta/\log\Delta -> modified log-Sobolev constant \Omega_{\Delta}(1/n)
- O(n^{19/9}\log q) for degree unbounded; spectral gap larger than n^{-10/9}
- holds for list coloring; Theorem 24
- edge colorings: q\geq(2+o(1))d; line graph degree up to 2d-2
- near ergodicity threshold: reducible when q<2d
- Vizing: edge colorable for q\geq d+1; rapid mixing under same condition known for trees

- Section 2 notation/preliminaries; Section 2.5 matrix trickle-down
- Section 3 construction + main results
- Section 4 analysis of inequalities, maybe of independent interest

steps.text:
A proper (vertex) q -coloring of a graph G=(V,E) assigns each vertex one of q colors so that adjacent vertices always get distinct colors. Let \Delta be the maximum degree of G. It is widely conjectured that the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling proper colorings on G uniformly mixes rapidly whenever the number of colors q is at least \Delta+2. The seminal work of Jerrum and Salas and Sokal showed that Glauber dynamics is rapidly mixing when q\geq 2\Delta, and after that a number of works tried to resolve the conjecture. The current best bound needs q\geq\left(\frac{11}{6}-\epsilon_{0}\right)\Delta for some \epsilon_{0}\approx 10^{-5}, and this is still far from what we want.

Another way to approach the conjecture is to look at special graph families, and the most successful cases are graphs with large girths. In a very recent work of Chen, Liu, Mani and Moitra, it was proven that for any \Delta\geq 3 there is a \mathrm{g}>0 such that for any graph G with maximum degree at most \Delta and girth at least \mathrm{g}, the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling proper q -colorings on G mixes rapidly whenever q\geq\Delta+3. This result almost solves the conjecture for large girth graphs.

A closely related problem is sampling proper edge colorings. Here the colors are assigned to the edges instead of the vertices, so that adjacent edges have distinct colors. A proper edge coloring of G corresponds naturally to a vertex coloring of the line graph of G, where the vertices are the edges of G and two vertices are adjacent in the line graph if and only if the corresponding edges are incident in G. So sampling proper colorings on line graphs is of particular interest. Graphs with a large girth are "locally sparse", but line graphs are "locally dense". A line graph is formed by gluing together several cliques, and each vertex belongs to exactly two cliques. Previous methods like coupling can hardly use this special structure, and so for a long time the rapid mixing condition for line graphs stayed the same as for general graphs.

In a recent breakthrough, Abdolazimi, Liu and Oveis Gharan developed a new technique for proving rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics, the matrix trickle-down theorem, which can make good use of the structural information of the underlying graphs. With it, it was shown in that work that the Glauber dynamics for sampling colorings on line graphs mixes rapidly when q>\frac{10}{6}\Delta. Together with the recent revolutionary development of the "local-to-global" scheme for high-dimensional expanders, the technique gives optimal mixing time for certain Markov chains. The matrix trickle-down theorem generalizes an earlier trickle-down theorem, which connected the spectral gaps of the local walks on links of the underlying simplicial complexes. The matrix version does not only look at the spectral gap but also at the local walks themselves, and it establishes more general connections between (the transition matrix of) local walks on links.

To apply the matrix trickle-down, one has to design suitable matrix upper bounds for the local walks and keep their spectrum bounded. These matrices also have to satisfy some inductive inequality constraints. Constructing these matrix upper bounds is the main technical challenge, because one needs precise control over the magnitudes of their eigenvalues. In this work, we study the constraints that come up in the matrix trickle-down theorem systematically and give an almost optimal construction of matrix upper bounds for sampling proper colorings on line graphs. Compared to the earlier construction, our construction has several advantages:

- Our construction of the matrix upper bound for each local walk is explicit.

- We relate the spectrum of each matrix upper bound directly to the spectrum of the adjacent matrix of the line graph, which is locally a clique and so is well-understood. This way we can get the desired spectrum bound in an improved regime.

- We reduce the existence of matrix upper bounds to whether a system of inequalities is feasible, and we give a complete characterization of that.

So we get an O_{\Delta}(n\log n) mixing time for colorings of bounded degree line graphs with o(\Delta) extra colors.

Let G=(V,E) be a line graph with n vertices and maximum degree \Delta. If q\geq\Delta+20028\cdot\Delta/\log\Delta, then the Glauber dynamics on the q -colorings of G has modified log-Sobolev constant \Omega_{\Delta}(1/n), and thus mixes in time O_{\Delta}(n\log n).

We also get an O(n^{19/9}\log q) mixing time on the family of line graphs where the degree is unbounded, with o(\Delta) extra colors.

Let G=(V,E) be a line graph with n vertices and maximum degree \Delta. If q\geq\Delta+20028\cdot\Delta/\log\Delta, then the Glauber dynamics on the q -colorings of G has spectral gap larger than n^{-10/9}, and thus mixes in time O(n^{19/9}\log q).

Actually, our proofs work for more general list coloring instances with o(\Delta) extra colors. Theorem 24 has the most general statement.

Our results can also be stated for sampling edge colorings. Then the rapid mixing condition is q\geq(2+o(1))d, where d is the maximum degree of the graph (the maximum degree of the corresponding line graph can be as large as 2d-2). This is close to the ergodicity threshold for the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling edge colorings, because it is known that the chain is reducible when q<2d. On the other side, by Vizing's theorem the graph is edge colorable whenever q\geq d+1, and rapid mixing under the same condition is known for trees.

In Section 2 we introduce the notations we need and some preliminary results, and in Section 2.5 we review the matrix trickle-down theorem. In Section 3 we describe our construction and prove the main results. Section 4 has a main ingredient of the proof, which is the analysis of the inequalities that arise in the matrix trickle-down theorem. This analysis might be of independent interest.

Combined with the recent revolutionary development of the "local-to-global" scheme for high-dimensional expanders [11,12], the technique yields optimal mixing time for certain Markov chains. The matrix trickle-down theorem is a generalization of the trickle-down theorem in [13], which established connections between the spectral gaps of the local walks on links of the underlying simplicial complexes. Instead of looking only at the spectral gap, the matrix trickle-down theorem takes the local walks themselves into account and establishes more general connections between (the transition matrices of) local walks on links.

To apply the matrix trickle-down theorem, one needs to design appropriate matrix upper bounds for the local walks while keeping their spectrum bounded, and these matrices must also satisfy certain inductive inequality constraints. Constructing these matrix upper bounds is the main technical challenge, since one needs precise control over the magnitudes of their eigenvalues. In this work, we systematically study the constraints arising in the matrix trickle-down theorem and provide an almost optimal construction of matrix upper bounds for sampling proper colorings on line graphs. Our construction has several advantages compared to the one in [10]:

- Our construction of the matrix upper bound for each local walk is explicit.

- We directly relate the spectrum of each matrix upper bound to that of the adjacent matrix of the line graph, which is locally a clique and therefore well-understood. This lets us obtain the desired spectrum bound in an improved regime.

- We reduce the existence of matrix upper bounds to the feasibility of a system of inequalities, for which we give a complete characterization.

As a result, we obtain an O_{\Delta}(n\log n) mixing time for bounded degree line graph colorings with o(\Delta) extra colors.

Let G=(V,E) be a line graph with n vertices and maximum degree \Delta. If q\geq\Delta+20028\cdot\Delta/\log\Delta, then the Glauber dynamics on the q -colorings of G has modified log-Sobolev constant \Omega_{\Delta}(1/n), and thus mixes in time O_{\Delta}(n\log n).

Moreover, we obtain an O(n^{19/9}\log q) mixing time on the (degree unbounded) family of line graphs with o(\Delta) extra colors.

Let G=(V,E) be a line graph with n vertices and maximum degree \Delta. If q\geq\Delta+20028\cdot\Delta/\log\Delta, then the Glauber dynamics on the q -colorings of G has spectral gap larger than n^{-10/9}, and thus mixes in time O(n^{19/9}\log q).

In fact, our proofs hold for more general list coloring instances with o(\Delta) extra colors; see Theorem 24 for the most general statement.

Our results can also be stated in terms of sampling edge colorings, in which case the rapid mixing condition becomes q\geq(2+o(1))d, where d is the maximum degree of the graph (note that the maximum degree of the corresponding line graph can be as large as 2d-2). This is close to the ergodicity threshold for the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling edge colorings, since the chain is known to be reducible when q<2d [14]. On the other hand, Vizing's theorem states that the graph is edge colorable whenever q\geq d+1, and rapid mixing under the same condition is known for trees [15].

We introduce the necessary notations and some preliminary results in Section 2, and review the matrix trickle-down theorem in Section 2.5. We then describe our construction and prove the main results in Section 3. A main ingredient of our proof, the analysis of the inequalities arising in the matrix trickle-down theorem, is presented in Section 4; this analysis might be of independent interest.
